concept: BarChart is a chart-recorder window on the unit: a ruled scale cut into the body, bars printed in ink on it, each told apart by a pattern and carrying its own number, so a person reads a table of values at a glance and every bar can also be reached with the arrow keys and read from a plain table.

default_to_avoid.pattern: bar chart in a dashboard card: one rounded bar per series in blue, green and orange, a legend of coloured dots and a tooltip that appears on hover
default_to_avoid.why_not: Series told apart by hue alone fail anyone who cannot see the hue, spend orange outside the one primary control, and a hover tooltip leaves keyboard users without the numbers.

default_to_avoid.pattern: chart drawn as a flat image or canvas with no text alternative
default_to_avoid.why_not: P4 says a mark that shows a value exposes it as text, so every bar must have its number printed, a readout and a table behind it.

references.source: Chart recorders and pen plotters of the 1960s: a ruled paper scale behind a window, marks printed in one ink
Braun T 1000 world receiver (Dieter Rams, 1963): a printed scale in a window read against ruled divisions
Edward Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information: label the marks directly and keep the ink for the data

derivation.consequence: the window is recessed into the body (inverse light)
derivation.form: The ruled scale and the bars sit in one recessed window with elevation.well and surface.sunken, so the chart reads as a display cut into the unit, not a card laid on it.

derivation.consequence: a lit level uses ink at full step, never orange
derivation.form: Every bar is outlined in full step ink and filled with ink or an ink pattern, so no series, bar or gridline uses action.accent or any hue.

derivation.consequence: exposes it as text to assistive tech
derivation.form: Each bar prints its number on itself, a live readout says the focused bar in words, and a visually hidden table holds every value for screen readers.

derivation.consequence: tabular numerals, a 7-segment face for LCD values
derivation.form: Axis numbers, bar values and the readout use tabular figures so a number keeps its width as the data changes.

derivation.consequence: arrows step a detent, Home and End reach the ends
derivation.form: The chart takes one tab stop; the arrow keys step bar by bar along the categories and across the series, and Home and End reach the first and the last category.
New data redraws the bars in place with no growing animation, so there is nothing to switch off under reduce motion.

derivation.consequence: ink on plastic at ≥4.5:1 in both themes
derivation.form: Axis numbers, category names and values are printed in text.primary or text.secondary on the sunken window, 8.4:1 and 6.0:1 in light and higher in dark.

options.name: bars with patterned fills in one recessed window, a ruled value scale and the value printed on each bar
ledger rows with dotted leaders and a thin patterned rule as the bar, no window and no scale
each bar built from a column of grille holes lit in ink up to the value, series told by hole shape

variants.reason: A keeps a ruled scale so values compare against a true zero, prints each number on its mark, and tells series apart by pattern in the one recessed display window P2 allows; B has no scale and is the horizontal case A already covers, and C gives only coarse hole steps with no printed value, which breaks P4's rule that a grille carries a reading as text.

root.why: The chart fills the inline size of its column and keeps its block size whatever the data says, so the layout does not reflow when values change.

header.why: The printed title sits on the inset line above the window, aligned to its start edge, like the label above a fader.

title.why: The title is printed in the label size and regular weight, flat ink with no emphasis, like the name above Meter.

svg.why: The drawing is the single tab stop of the chart and takes the arrow, Home and End keys, with no tab stop per bar.

window.why: The plot is a recess with inverse light and a hairline edge in line.ring that holds 3:1 against the body, at a fixed block size so a hover or a focus never moves the chart.

grid.why: Value gridlines are dashed hairlines of printing across the window, a different shape from the solid bar outlines.

base.why: The zero line is the one solid hairline in the window, so every bar visibly starts from the same true zero.

tick.why: The value-axis numbers are tabular figures at the caption size in secondary ink, the same printing as a fader scale.

cat.why: Category names are printed at the caption size in regular weight under or beside their group, never inside a bar.

bar.why: A bar is a rectangle outlined in full step ink and filled with an ink pattern, so series differ by texture and not by hue.

hit.why: A transparent band over each category column gives a pointer a target at least as wide as the column, larger than the bars it covers.

value.why: Each bar prints its value at its end in medium weight and tabular figures, so no one reads a number off the scale.

focusMark.why: The keyboard mark is a ring drawn round the active bar with a gap, in the focus ring ink, so focus is a shape round the part and not a tint.

legend.why: The legend lists every series by name beside its own pattern swatch, so the pattern is decoded in words.

key.why: Each legend entry puts the swatch and the name on one line at the same height, aligned to the inset line.

swatch.why: The swatch is a small copy of the series pattern in an outlined rectangle, the same shape as the bar so it matches without hue.

name.why: The series name is printed at the caption size in primary ink, regular weight.

readout.why: The readout is a polite live region under the window that says the focused bar in words, such as Tue, Hot water: 7 kWh, and is never a control.

table.why: A real table of the same numbers is clipped out of sight and kept for assistive tech, so the data never lives only in the drawing.

tileBg.why: The ground of every pattern tile is the sunken surface, so the hatch, the dots and the lines read as printing on the recess.

tileInk.why: Hatch and line patterns are strokes of full step ink at the ring width, a texture that survives a greyscale print.

tileDot.why: The dot pattern uses full step ink discs, a third texture next to the hatch and the lines.

tileSolid.why: The solid pattern is a full step ink fill, the one dense texture, so the first series stands out against the lighter ones.

data-active.why: The active bar, from keys or a pointer, takes a ring-width outline in place of the hairline, a cue that is a line weight and not a colour.

data-idle.why: Before any bar is active the readout shows the key hint in secondary ink, and the value in primary ink once one is.

focus-visible.why: The focus ring round the active bar is drawn only when the keyboard has focus, so a pointer press does not leave a ring.

@media forced-colors: active.why: In forced colours the window, bars, patterns and the ring use system colours so the data and the active bar survive.
